subject: Svenska 2
title: Oral presentation and presentation technique
sourceSummary: Adapting a speech to its audience and purpose, rhetorical aids in speech, handling nerves and questions, and visual aids.

questions.prompt: A student is to give the same speech about climate change to both their own class and to younger pupils in year 4. What should mainly be adapted between the two occasions?
questions.opener: What does a ten-year-old know about the climate issue that an upper-secondary student already knows?
choices: Nothing, the same speech works for any audience
Only the length of the speech, not the content
Word choice, examples and level of detail based on the audience's prior knowledge
The speaker's clothing, but nothing else
questions.explanation: Good audience adaptation means adjusting word choice, examples, level of detail and sometimes structure to the audience's age, prior knowledge and interests — otherwise the speech risks becoming incomprehensible or uninteresting.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a common purpose to start from when planning a speech?
questions.opener: Three are about what the speech should achieve — one is about something else entirely.
choices: To avoid eye contact
To inform
To persuade
To entertain
questions.explanation: A speech is usually planned based on the purpose of informing, persuading or entertaining (often a combination). Eye contact is a matter of presentation technique, not a purpose of the speech.

questions.prompt: Which rhetorical device involves deliberately creating a brief silence before an important message in order to build tension?
questions.opener: What happens to the audience's attention just before you say the most important thing?
choices: Antithesis
Anaphora
Dispositio
A dramatic pause
questions.explanation: A dramatic pause is used deliberately to build tension, give the audience time to absorb information, or emphasise what comes next. Antithesis and anaphora are figures of speech in the language itself, not in the delivery.

questions.prompt: What is meant by prosody in oral presentation?
questions.opener: It is about HOW something sounds, not what is said.
choices: The written structure of the text
The voice's variation in pitch, tempo and stress
The number of figures of speech in the speech
The composition of the audience
questions.explanation: Prosody refers to the variation of the voice — pitch, tempo, stress and pauses — which is crucial for how a message is perceived and how it engages listeners, regardless of the quality of the content.

questions.prompt: Which method is most often recommended for handling nervousness before an oral presentation?
questions.opener: What actually tends to reduce nervousness most — improvisation or preparation?
choices: Avoiding all preparation in order to seem spontaneous
Reading the whole speech aloud without looking up
Thorough preparation, breathing exercises, and rehearsing the delivery in advance
Speaking as fast as possible to get it over with
questions.explanation: Thorough preparation and rehearsing the delivery in advance is the most effective method against nervousness, often combined with breathing exercises. Reading aloud without eye contact or speaking too fast instead makes the delivery worse.

questions.prompt: What is a common pitfall when using slides (for example PowerPoint) to support a speech?
questions.opener: What competes for the audience's attention if a slide has too much text?
choices: The slides become so full of text that the audience reads instead of listening to the speaker
The slides have too few words
No slides are used at all
The slideshow is displayed in the wrong colour
questions.explanation: A common mistake is filling the slides with too much text, which makes the audience read instead of listening to the speaker. Visual aids should complement the speech with key words, images or diagrams — not replace the spoken word.

questions.prompt: After a speech about the school's grading system, the speaker is asked a critical question they do not have an obvious answer to. Describe how the speaker can best handle the situation.
questions.opener: Which is worse — admitting uncertainty or bluffing?
questions.answer: The speaker should acknowledge that the question is relevant, answer honestly if there is uncertainty, reason from what they actually know, and possibly offer to come back with a more complete answer — rather than bluffing or becoming defensive.
steps: Listen to the whole question and acknowledge that it is relevant and interesting, to show respect for the person asking.
If the answer is not entirely clear, it is better to say so honestly than to bluff — credibility (ethos) is damaged more by an obviously false answer.
Reason from what you actually know or believe, and be clear about what is fact and what is your own reflection.
If needed, the speaker can offer to come back with a more thorough answer later, which shows a sense of responsibility rather than making the uncertainty look like a weakness.

questions.prompt: Summarise important presentation-technique concepts for oral presentation.
questions.opener: Voice, gaze, image and preparation — four pieces of the puzzle for a good speech.
questions.answer: Audience adaptation: word choice, examples and level of detail based on the audience's prior knowledge and age · Prosody: the voice's pitch, tempo, stress and pauses · Dramatic pause: deliberate silence to create tension or reflection · Visual aids: should complement the speech with key words and images, not be filled with long lines of text · Nervousness: best countered with thorough preparation and rehearsal, not by avoiding preparation · Q&A: honesty and calm handling of uncertainty strengthens credibility more than a bluffed answer.

questions.prompt: What should a speaker keep in mind when the purpose of the speech is to persuade rather than to inform?
questions.opener: A persuasive speech needs more than just facts to land.
choices: To clearly formulate a thesis and back it up with arguments aimed at the audience's values
To just list facts with no clear line of argument
To avoid all emotional language
To never address counterarguments
questions.explanation: A persuasive speech should have a clear thesis backed up with arguments tailored to the audience's values and interests, and preferably also address likely counterarguments. Just listing facts with no through-line or avoiding emotional language makes the speech less persuasive.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of using concrete examples and stories (anecdotes) in a speech?
questions.opener: Consider what's easier to remember: an abstract principle or a concrete story.
choices: To make abstract ideas more understandable and engaging for the audience
To lengthen the speech with no real purpose
To avoid needing a clear thesis
Anecdotes are never used in serious speeches
questions.explanation: Concrete examples and anecdotes make abstract ideas more understandable, memorable and engaging for the audience. They are widely used even in serious, well-regarded speeches, not just to fill time.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a common physical breathing technique that can reduce nervousness before a speech?
questions.opener: Think about which type of breathing calms the nervous system.
choices: Slow, deep breathing from the stomach
Holding your breath for as long as possible
Breathing extremely fast right before the speech
Avoiding conscious breathing altogether
questions.explanation: Slow, deep breathing from the stomach (diaphragmatic breathing) helps calm the nervous system and can reduce nervousness before a speech. Holding your breath or breathing extremely fast instead makes the body more stressed.

questions.prompt: What is an advantage of using an image or a diagram instead of a long line of text in a slideshow?
questions.opener: Think about what the audience should be paying attention to: the speaker or the screen.
choices: An image can convey information quickly and support the spoken word without competing with it for attention
Images always make a speech more confusing
Images can never replace text
Diagrams are only suitable in scientific subjects
questions.explanation: An image or a diagram can convey information quickly and visually, which supports the spoken word instead of competing with it for the audience's attention, as long lines of text otherwise do. Diagrams can, moreover, be useful in many different subjects, not just scientific ones.

questions.prompt: A speaker is to present the same research findings to both experts in the field and the general public. What should differ the most between the two versions?
questions.opener: Think about what background knowledge the two groups already have.
choices: The level of technical language and how much background is explained
The speaker's vocal volume
The length of every single sentence should always be identical
There is no reason to change anything at all
questions.explanation: With experts, the speaker can use technical language and go straight to the results, while a presentation for the general public should explain more background and avoid unnecessary jargon to be understandable.

questions.prompt: What is the deliberate choice to vary the voice's volume and tempo to hold the audience's attention called?
questions.opener: This concept is about the voice as a tool, not about word choice itself.
choices: Vocal variety (part of prosody)
A written-language aid
A figure of speech in the text
A type of source handling
questions.explanation: Vocal variety, which is part of prosody, means deliberately varying the voice's volume, tempo and pitch to hold the audience's attention and emphasise important parts of the speech.

questions.prompt: What can be an advantage of rehearsing a speech out loud for others before the real occasion?
questions.opener: Think about what a test audience can give you that you don't get from just reading through the speech silently.
choices: You get feedback and can adjust content, tempo and body language before the real speech
It's only a waste of time
It makes the speaker more nervous than if they hadn't rehearsed at all
It replaces the need to actually know the content
questions.explanation: Rehearsing out loud for others gives concrete feedback on content, tempo, clarity and body language, allowing the speaker to adjust the speech before the real occasion. Rehearsal usually reduces nervousness rather than increasing it, but it doesn't replace the need to actually know the content.
